preamble: Pasquale March 7 Wordplay in each of the down clues contains a superfluous letter. In clue order, these spell out an instruction to remove six unpleasant figures from the completed grid before submitting your entry.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unsuccessful type turning red, ultimately betrayed again?

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so the word for the failure is read from its end

parts.note: an unsuccessful person is a loser

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the colour is used

parts.note: the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: A failed type turns red with shame, having been sold out once more.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: betrayed as in sold down the river, so betrayed again is sold again.
explanation.definitionFit: To sell someone out is to betray them, so goods or people sold a second time are punningly betrayed again.

clue.text: Once again evaluate fools interrupting revolutionary prophet

indicators.note: something interrupting breaks into the middle, so the fools go inside
a revolution turns things round, so the word for the prophet is read backwards

parts.note: a seer foresees the future; one of its Es is this clue's superfluous letter
asses are fools

explanation.surface: A disillusioned prophet, surrounded by idiots, takes another look at things.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the wordplay gives one letter too many: REASSESES. The surplus E is the first letter of the hidden instruction ERASE SPLIT DEVILS.
explanation.definitionFit: To reassess is to assess, judge or appraise something a second time.

clue.text: Seemly Parisian on one piece of furniture

parts.note: sur is French for on; its R is this clue's superfluous letter
I is the Roman numeral one
a table is a piece of furniture

explanation.surface: A Parisian perched decorously on a piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives SURITABLE; the surplus R is the second letter of the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Seemly means proper or appropriate to the occasion, which is what suitable means.

clue.text: Beer given to a king over time — waste, if liquid

parts.note: ale is beer; its A is this clue's superfluous letter
taken as written
K is the chess abbreviation for king
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Beer handed to a monarch over the years goes to waste if it is spilled.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives ALEAKAGE; dropping the surplus first A, third letter of the instruction, leaves the answer. 'Over' just places the age last.
explanation.definitionFit: Leakage is the loss of liquid seeping out, so it is a waste when the thing lost is a fluid.

clue.text: No idea about Native American people

indicators.note: about can mean turned around or in disarray, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone admits they know nothing about a particular Native American nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oneida are an Iroquoian nation originally from what is now upstate New York, one of the Six Nations.

clue.text: Part of church chosen as vestry — outsiders kicked out

indicators.note: the outsiders are kicked out, so the letters at the back of the phrase are thrown away too
with kicked out, the letters on the outside of the phrase, at its front, are thrown away

parts.note: the run left in the middle of these words, read straight through, gives the answer plus one spare letter

explanation.surface: A vestry is picked to serve as part of the church, with outsiders thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outsiders' drops CHOSE, leaving NASVESTRY, and 'kicked out' drops STRY, leaving NASVE; its S is this clue's superfluous letter for the preamble's message, so it goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The nave is the central body of a church building where the congregation sits.

clue.text: Hostility one meets with Bard outside 'orrible place

indicators.note: outside says the pair formed by one and the Bard goes around the 'orrible place, enclosing it

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
the Bard is Shakespeare, whose first name is Will
'orrible place is hell with its H dropped, Cockney-style, giving 'ELL

explanation.surface: Someone meets Shakespeare outside a horrible place and feels nothing but hostility.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says every down clue's wordplay carries one spare letter; here it is the E of the Cockney hell, and it is the fifth letter of the hidden instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill will is a common phrase for a feeling of enmity or malice toward someone, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Presents special forces to protect part of hospital

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding it, so the forces go around the hospital part

parts.note: the SAS is the British Special Air Service; its first S is the superfluous letter
a ward is a room or section of a hospital

explanation.surface: Special forces are given gifts for guarding a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives SAWARDS; the surplus first S starts the second word of the instruction, SPLIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Awards are prizes handed over to people, so they are presents in the sense of things given.

clue.text: A misleading statement about pop instrument

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about here means going around, so the untruth wraps itself round the parent

parts.note: a lie is a statement meant to mislead
pop is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: Someone tells a fib about a pop instrument, perhaps a guitar or synth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' suggests pop music, but it is the father; the instrument is a surveying one, not a musical one.
explanation.definitionFit: An alidade is a sighting device used in surveying and astronomy for measuring angles, so it is a scientific instrument.

clue.text: Writers full of extraordinary magic putting out 100 puzzles

indicators.note: the writers' word holds the other letters inside it, as a container is full of its contents

parts.note: writers are pens; the P of pens is this clue's superfluous letter, which the preamble removes

indicators.note: something extraordinary is out of the ordinary, so the letters of magic are rearranged
one letter is removed from the word magic, as if put out of it

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: Writers steeped in remarkable magic, without a hundred of something, produce puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: Writers are PENS, but the preamble's superfluous letter here is the P, leaving ENS. 'Putting out' C (100) from MAGIC leaves MAGI, 'extraordinary' rearranges it, and ENS is 'full of' the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Enigmas are mysteries or riddles, things that puzzle people, so a plural synonym.

clue.text: Criminal resident in foul community

indicators.note: a resident lives inside a place, so the convict sits inside the word for nasty

parts.note: foul and vile both mean disgusting
an old lag is a habitual criminal in British slang

explanation.surface: A crook is living in some squalid little settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: LAG is British slang for a convict, as in 'old lag'.
explanation.definitionFit: A village is a small rural settlement and the people living in it, so it serves as a community.

clue.text: Vessel left on river invaded by sheep

indicators.note: the sheep's letters force their way inside the pair of letters, as an invader enters territory
in a down clue one piece sits on top of the next, so the first comes before the second

parts.note: a ewe is a female sheep

explanation.surface: A boat left on a river finds itself overrun by sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: L on R, invaded by EWE, gives LEWER; the preamble's spare letter here is the L, which goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug or pitcher, a container for water, so a vessel in the sense of receptacle.

clue.text: Dealing with good and evil spirits has disturbed fellow in charge

definitions.text: Dealing with good and evil spirits

indicators.note: disturbed means thrown out of order, so the letters of the little verb before it are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a fellow is a man
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A man in authority has been troubled by dealings with the spirit world.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaman mediates between people and the spirit world, so shamanic practice deals with both benevolent and malign spirits.

clue.text: Child that is following captain in story

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the abbreviation is placed behind the pirate's name

parts.note: Captain William Kidd, the pirate of legend and story
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A child follows the captain about in some tale of adventure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' puts the first block of words after the second, so the captain comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiddie is an informal, affectionate word for a young child.

clue.text: Sporting award is sent back, getting marvelled about

indicators.note: sending something back returns it the way it came, so the little word is read right to left

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

indicators.note: about signals the letters being moved around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sporting trophy is returned, and everyone is amazed by it.
explanation.definitionFit: Second place in Olympic and similar competitions is rewarded with a medal of the second precious metal.

clue.text: Upset archbishop is associated with this writer's sort of philosophy

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the archbishop's name reads from the bottom up

parts.note: William Laud was Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I
taken as written
this writer is the setter, and this writer's is I'm, I am; one of its Is is the superfluous letter

explanation.surface: An archbishop is upset to find himself associated with the setter's philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives DUALISIM; the surplus I is the fourth letter of SPLIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Dualism is the philosophical doctrine that reality has two basic kinds, such as mind and matter.

clue.text: Fruit scheme has blemish

parts.note: a scheme is a plan
a taint is a stain or blemish; its final T is the superfluous letter

explanation.surface: A fruit-growing scheme turns out to be flawed.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives PLANTAINT; the surplus T completes SPLIT.
explanation.definitionFit: The plantain is a starchy banana-like fruit, usually cooked before eating.

clue.text: Dry river garment that gets wet

parts.note: to drain something is to dry it; its D is this clue's superfluous letter
the Wear is a river in north-east England, flowing through Durham and Sunderland

explanation.surface: Someone drains a river, puzzlingly, while their clothes get soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives DRAINWEAR; the surplus D starts DEVILS. 'Dry' and 'wet' are set against each other to confuse.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainwear is waterproof clothing worn in wet weather, so it is the clothing that gets rained on.

clue.text: Spanish music a special gala's organised, putting English learner off

indicators.note: the letters are put into a new order, as something organised is rearranged
with off, this says the named letters are put off, removed from the pool before rearranging
with putting, the named letters are taken off the pool of letters, removed before rearranging

parts.note: these words supply the letters to be rearranged
L is for learner, as on a learner driver's L-plate

explanation.surface: A special gala's programme is arranged, with an English learner sent off stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting English learner off' removes E and L from the letters of A SPECIAL GALAS, and 'organised' rearranges the rest into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A passacaglia is a slow stately dance form, originally Spanish, built over a repeating bass line.

clue.text: French father and mother collecting third of this bounty

indicators.note: collecting something means gathering it in, so the letter goes inside the mother

parts.note: pere is French for father; its middle E is the superfluous letter
mum is mother

indicators.note: the third of a word is its third letter, the only one used

parts.note: the third letter of this word

explanation.surface: A French father and mother gather up a third of the reward.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives PEREMIUM; the surplus E is the second letter of DEVILS.
explanation.definitionFit: A premium is a bonus or extra payment, and a bounty is likewise a reward paid out.

clue.text: Worker somewhere in Austria — I put out a feeler

indicators.note: to put something out is to eject it, so the letter named just before goes

parts.note: a worker ant, the crossword's usual worker
Vienna is Austria's capital; its V is the superfluous letter
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: An ant working somewhere in Austria announces that it is sending out a feeler.
explanation.walkthrough: VIENNA without I gives VENNA, so the wordplay gives ANTVENNA; the surplus V is the third letter of DEVILS.
explanation.definitionFit: An antenna is an insect's sensory organ on the head, also called a feeler.

clue.text: Is taxi worker defying the union?

parts.note: taken as written; its I is the superfluous letter
a cab is a taxi

explanation.surface: A question: is this taxi driver breaking the strike?
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives ISCAB; the surplus I is the fourth letter of DEVILS.
explanation.definitionFit: A scab is a strikebreaker, someone who keeps working against the wishes of their trade union.

clue.text: Blossoming science establishment to appear out of nowhere?

parts.note: a lab, laboratory, is a scientific workplace; its first letter is the superfluous one
something that looms appears suddenly and menacingly

explanation.surface: A science facility seems to spring up from nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives LABLOOM; the surplus L is the fifth letter of DEVILS.
explanation.definitionFit: Abloom means in flower, so a plant that is abloom is blossoming.

clue.text: Sign of poor cleaning you and I found in cold old B&B

indicators.note: something found in a place is inside it, so the pronoun sits between the two Bs

parts.note: C for cold, as on taps
O is the abbreviation for old
the two Bs of the abbreviation, split to hold the pronoun
you and I together are we

explanation.surface: We stayed in a cold, old-fashioned bed and breakfast that showed signs of poor housekeeping.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobweb left hanging in a corner shows that a room has not been dusted properly.

clue.text: Eavesdrop, being strangely silent at home

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd way, so the letters that follow come out in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Someone stays quiet at home, the better to overhear what is said.
explanation.definitionFit: To listen in is to overhear a conversation or tap a phone line, which is what eavesdropping means.

clue.text: Going round lake, observes fish

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so the verb surrounds the letter

parts.note: to observe is to see; its first S is the superfluous letter
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Someone walks round a lake watching the fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives SEELS; the surplus S ends DEVILS. The instruction is to erase six devils split across the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Eels are long snake-like fish found in rivers and the sea.

clue.text: Trite remark when woman at match receives honour

indicators.note: to receive is to take in, so the honour goes inside the woman

parts.note: a match is a marriage, and the woman marrying is the bride
the OM, Order of Merit, is a British honour

explanation.surface: A woman at a sporting match is handed an award and says something banal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' suggests sport, but it is a marriage. The OM is the Order of Merit, an honour given by the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Bromide was a sedative, so a bromide came to mean a dull, soothing platitude or commonplace remark.

clue.text: Monet excited when framing a good piece of art

indicators.note: a frame goes around a picture, so the rearranged name surrounds the two letters
excited means stirred up, so the painter's name is shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Monet gets excited when he frames a fine painting.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes Monet the artist, but his name is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A montage is a composite artwork made by assembling pieces of other pictures or film.

clue.text: Plant end being twisted, hiding another plant mostly

indicators.note: to hide something is to cover it, so the shortened plant goes inside
a word being twisted round faces the other way, so it is read backwards

parts.note: an end is a purpose or aim

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter of the second plant is dropped

parts.note: moss is a small flowerless plant

explanation.surface: A gardener twists the end of one plant to hide most of another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End' looks like the tip of a stem, but it means an aim or goal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimosa is a genus of plants including the sensitive plant; the name is also used for yellow-flowered acacias.

clue.text: Old coin — the way edge has worn away

indicators.note: a worn edge is lost, so the word for the way loses its first letter

parts.note: t' is the northern English dialect form of the
a way of doing something is a manner

explanation.surface: An old coin, its rim worn smooth by years of handling.
explanation.walkthrough: A worn edge suits an old coin, but here the edge is a word's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tanner was the British slang name for the old sixpence coin, withdrawn after decimalisation.
